Grade 3-5

Student treats numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers, so 1/8 looks bigger than 1/4 because 8 > 4.

HIGH
Grade 3-5

1/2 + 1/3 → 2/5. Student adds the parts of each fraction independently.

▶
Fractions must be less than 1
MEDIUM
Grade 3-5

Student rejects improper fractions (5/4, 7/3) as "wrong" or impossible.

▶
Fractions are not numbers
MEDIUM
Grade 3-5

Student treats 3/4 as a "relationship" or "command" rather than as a point on the number line with a specific magnitude.

▶
Equivalence ≠ same magnitude
MEDIUM
Grade 3-5

Student can compute equivalent fractions procedurally (multiply top and bottom by 2) but does not believe they represent the same amount.

▶
Multiplication always makes things bigger
MEDIUM
Grade 4-6

Student is surprised that 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4, since 1/4 < 1/2.

▶
Division always makes things smaller
MEDIUM
Grade 4-6

Student is surprised that 4 ÷ 1/2 = 8, since 8 > 4.

▶
Adding without a common denominator
HIGH
Grade 4-5

Student does not realize that fractions must have the same denominator (or same-size pieces) before they can be added or subtracted.

▶
Simplification by subtraction
LOW
Grade 4-5

Student tries to simplify by subtracting instead of dividing: e.g., simplifies 6/8 to 4/6 by subtracting 2 from both.

▶
Mixed number arithmetic errors
MEDIUM
Grade 4-5

When adding mixed numbers (2 1/4 + 1 3/4), student adds whole parts and fractional parts separately without regrouping (gets 3 4/4 = 3 instead of 4).

▶
Percent ↔ decimal misplacement
MEDIUM
Grade 5-6

Student writes 25% as 0.025 or 2.5 instead of 0.25; treats the percent sign as decimal moves of varying length.

▶
Unit fraction misconception
MEDIUM
Grade 3-4

Student does not see 3/4 as 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4. Treats 3/4 as a single indivisible quantity.
